content.thinking:
I'm thinking the Overwatch aesthetic calls for polished sci-fi shapes with panel lines and bold color blocking, maybe borrowing from Talon's tech vibe, and considering how to render a kraken with a semi-mechanical, armored look rather than organic tentacles alone.

Settling on deep navy-teal body with cream undersides and a vivid orange-gold accent for glowing eyes and armor bands, plus bioluminescent stripes and beveled panel trim on the mantle. I'm working out the pose too: a rising kraken emerging from a water-disc base at y=0, mantle around 5m tall with tentacles spanning roughly 10m, some curling upward dramatically while others drape across the water's surface.

Now I'm planning the skeleton hierarchy -- a core root joint near the body base, with a spine chain running up through the tilted mantle toward the head, eyes and funnel at the front, and tentacles radiating from the front-bottom around the mouth.

I'm adding a funnel tube below the head and a beak with jointed upper/lower jaws at the mouth. For tentacles, I'm planning 8 arms radiating around the mouth as jointed chains, with 6 spread outward, 2 curled upward, plus 2 longer feeding tentacles with club tips, for ten total.

Tallying joints across arms, feeding tentacles, mantle spine, head, jaws, eyes, and fins keeps me around 85, comfortably under the 160 limit. I'm now working out tentacle geometry with tapering radii and octagonal cross-sections, plus countershading colors (dark navy-teal top, cream/cyan underside) and sucker details placed along sweep frames, trying to merge geometry by color to minimize part count.

Since the part budget caps around 1000, I'm rethinking sucker density—maybe limiting real geometric suckers to the big arms (around 10 per arm × 8 arms = 80 parts) using small low-poly torus rings in cream color to represent the cups, rather than individually sticking hundreds of parts across all tentacles.

I'm considering placing suckers only where visible: inner sides of raised arms and curled tips, since grounded arms hide their suckers underwater against the surface, which saves on part count while keeping the realistic look where it matters.

For the color palette, I'm aiming for that clean Overwatch aesthetic—smooth gradient shading rather than mottled texture, with a deep indigo-blue body, lighter cyan-blue accents, and glowing orange highlight lines for energy details.

Now I'm thinking through the armor concept: a sci-fi kraken with ridged armored plates around the mantle and a plated head, with the hot orange used sparingly for eyes, glow stripes, tentacle tip bands, and sucker glow—keeping that strong blue/orange complementary contrast.

Writing tentacle cuff geometry...

Switching to estimating part counts, roughly 17 parts per tentacle times 10 for cuffs, suckers, and sweeps, totaling around 170. I'm also thinking through how to render a stylized water base disc since true translucency isn't available.

For the water effect I'm picturing teal-cyan coloring with white foam rings, splash crest spikes arranged around the body's base, foam tori at each tentacle root, and scattered droplet spheres merged into one part. Since there's no skeleton, I need to decide how water elements bind to a joint — leaning toward naming the root joint "core" at the body's center so the water parts and flex tests all attach there properly.

Now I'm planning out the layout: body centered at x=0,z=0, mouth near [0,1.35,0.55], tentacle roots forming a ring around the head's underside at radius ~0.9. The head/body is a large ovoid stretching from y=1.2 up to a mantle tip at [0,5.2,-2.2], with eight tentacles spaced around the base at y~1.5, each one arcing outward and down to curl against the water surface at y~0.15, sized so the roots naturally rest at the correct height.

For the water contact, I want the arm centers to sit mostly above the thin glassy disc (top around y=0.14-0.2), undulating in gentle S-curves—rising up to about a meter at crests and dipping back toward the water at troughs—so they read as emerging tentacles rather than fully submerged ones, keeping any sink within the 2% height tolerance.

Now I'm laying out the arm positions around the kraken's body: eight arms spaced at roughly ±25°, ±65°, ±105°, and ±145° from the forward axis, with the front-facing pairs spread toward the viewer, the side pairs curling outward and upward, and the back pairs lying low across the water. I'm also planning two longer feeding tentacles raised higher and spread wider than the rest.

I'm building a coordinate system for each arm using a root point, a radial direction, a perpendicular swing direction, and height, then defining control-point profiles for a "lying" arm type that droops down and outward from the body into the water.

But the resulting scale seems too large -- arms spanning six meters with a total creature width of fifteen meters would make the main character tiny in the frame, so I need to scale everything down.

I'm planning the torso as a swept shape along a spine chain, with a rounded bottom cap around radius 0.95, and the arms emerging from a skirt at the base where their roots sit just inside the body radius.

Then I'm mapping out the spine path from the lower body up to a tapering tip, with varying tube radii to shape a mantle that bulges in the middle and narrows sharply at both ends — more like a kraken rising vertically with a tilted, pointed back than a simple cone.

Mantle radius tapers from 0.85 up to 1.15 near the collar then down to 0.1 at the tip, with a gunmetal collar ring at the head/mantle junction accented by an orange light line. For eyes, I'm placing large angled spheres on each side of the head with a gunmetal socket ring and a glowing orange iris with a dark horizontal slit pupil, going for that Overwatch-kraken look.

Working through how to apply the eye decal: an ivory-amber sclera sphere with an iris/pupil decal mapped on top, glowing only where the drawing exists so the pupil and iris pop against the lighter eyeball.

Now I'm sketching the iris SVG itself—a radial gradient orange-to-yellow circle, a dark rounded pupil rect, a white highlight, and a ring—then positioning each eye decal so it faces outward and slightly forward on the sphere's surface. I'm also planning angled brow plates in gunmetal with an orange stripe above each eye socket, plus a torus-shaped rim framing the eyeball.

I'm adding armored details across the head: a swept visor-like crest connecting the eyes, orange glowing accent lines, and several gunmetal rib rings spaced along the mantle, each built as a lathe band following the tangent of the body's spine curve.

I'm pairing ribs with hexagonal cross-sections — a gunmetal rib alongside a thinner orange glow strip for each segment, doubling the part count, and now considering adding a dorsal keel ridge along the mantle's top.

For the crest, I'm shaping a membrane between two mantle lines to form a sail-like fin in gunmetal/blue, and I'm also planning two lateral diamond-shaped fins extruded near the mantle tip.

Writing fin orientation code...

Still shaping tentacle colors...

Now I'm thinking about overall body shading in an Overwatch-style clean palette—navy dorsal, lighter blue flanks, cream belly with soft countershading, plus subtle panel-seam lines for a crisp armored look.

Writing mantle paint function...

Writing color gradient logic...

I'm adding gunmetal cuff rings with thin orange glow bands along the tentacles, then planning sucker placement on the underside—alternating zigzag rows tapering in size with the tube radius, built as small lathe-cup parts stuck onto the geometry.

Defining the lathe cup profile...

Working out the normal rule confirms the winding direction: moving outward gives a downward-facing normal, moving upward gives outward, which matches the floor and wall orientations I need. I'm also considering whether to just use the lathe SDK helper with the outline directly rather than hand-deriving each segment's orientation.

Keeping the sucker cups simple with cream coloring rather than adding an orange glow detail for now, and starting to plan the two feeding tentacles — longer and thinner than the arms, arcing up and out to the sides before curving toward clubbed, spiked, glowing-orange tips.

I'm reconsidering the overall height so the tentacle tips don't tower too far above the mantle, and sketching the curling paths for the four raised arms using a series of control points that sweep upward then spiral inward at the tips.

I'm also working out the geometry budget: each tentacle chain gets 6-7 joints, ring spacing roughly every 10 degrees, and 8-sided sweeps to keep the triangle count near 60k. For the full set of eight arms, I'm defining their azimuth angles mirrored left and right from the +Z axis, alternating the lateral curl direction between neighboring arms.

Now I'm sketching distinct poses per angle: a front pair reaching toward the viewer with curling tips, a raised arcing pair, a feeding pair stretching outward and high, a lying pair resting flat, and a back pair curling backward -- aiming for five arm types per side, ten total, blending octopus and decapod-style limbs.

Working out the arm root positions relative to the mantle center, computing coordinates with azimuth and radius offsets so each arm anchors properly into the head/mantle geometry, then starting to define the mantle spine curve from its base point upward.

I'm also planning the webbing skirt between the arm roots — a flared lathe collar extending from a narrower radius near the top down to a wider flare near the bottom, forming a thin shaded shell to connect the arms visually under the body.

Now I'm shifting to the base: a flat lathe disc for the water surface, with a slightly raised rim and foam ring details to sell the sense of something emerging from the sea.

Computing spike positions with trig for outward-tilted cones around the splash crown, accepting that some will overlap arms for a natural splash look. I'll keep radius roughly 1.7-2.1 and not worry about perfect spacing relative to arm angles.

For the orange accents, I'm planning glowing mantle strips along the flanks at ±40° to pair with the eyes, considering whether to replace or complement the existing painted accent line with glow sweeps on both sides of the seam.

I also want bioluminescent nodes—small glowing orange discs placed evenly along the mantle at ±75° per side—plus cuff rings on the arms, tentacle tip bands, an orange-edged beak against dark gunmetal, and possibly a small forward-facing funnel or jet nozzle below the chin as an optional detail.

I'm skipping the funnel to avoid crowding near the beak, and instead focusing on the beak itself: a jaw joint hinged below the head, with a hooked upper beak swept from a curved path and tapering to a point.

Shaping beak curve...

I'm checking for collisions between the beak position and the front arm roots, adjusting the arm angle and root radius so the arms don't overlap the beak geometry, and considering raising the beak slightly higher than the arm root height to clear the conflict.

Now I'm placing the head as an ellipsoid positioned forward and above the mantle, working out how the sphere's surface extends past the mantle's radius to form a bulb shape, and positioning the eyes partly embedded into the head sphere near the front.

I'll skip detailed brow stripes for now and focus on crest horns instead — adding a pair of swept-back armor horn plates behind the eyes, curved from brow to tip using a bezier sweep with tapering radius, rendered as gunmetal spikes with orange trim, accepting they may overlap the raised arms.

For the mantle, I'm adding armor shell plates on the sides plus a collar frill — a big gunmetal torus ring at the head/mantle junction glowing orange. Checking overall size: roughly 5.2m tall with the feeding tentacle and arms spanning about 11m wide including the water disc, which seems reasonable before moving to the skeleton setup with base, core, and mantle spine chain joints.

Now I'm continuing the skeleton: adding a head joint off the core, a jaw joint off the head for the beak, eye joints (eyeL/eyeR) as children of the head, and fin chains attached to the mantle with their own role assignments.

Writing fin and tentacle joint chains...

I'm defining the arm sweep using a radius function that tapers from thick at the root to thin at the tip, making sure the path height stays above the radius so the arms don't dip below the water surface near their base.

I need to double-check the mirroring math for the lateral offset vector—flipping the azimuth angle doesn't simply mirror the side vector, so I have to track the sign carefully to keep arms symmetric across left and right.

I'll keep the rest pose symmetric for clean, Overwatch-style aesthetics. Now I'm plotting the arm's curve points: starting near the shoulder, tapering down in radius along its length, then curling upward at the tip, with the arm spanning roughly 6 units and reaching out about 5 units laterally.

Checking that it stays within the water disc's radius of 5.6, and confirming the lateral offsets line up correctly at each point along the arm.

Now I'm plotting the second arm arcing upward and over before dipping back toward the water, and starting the curve for the third, raised arm that bends up and forward.

Finishing arm C's curl near the mantle height, then laying out arm D arcing back low before its tip curls upward, and beginning the thin feeding tentacle with a slender stalk leading to a club-shaped end.

Checking tip radius with a rounded cap, then figuring out arm root placement — attaching all arms at the same radial distance but spacing them by angle so they don't overlap too much where they meet the body.

Now I'm setting up the chain parameters: using 7 segments per arm, so total joint count comes to roughly 95 across the figure. For cuffs, I'm defining a lathe profile banded around each arm segment, sizing the radius slightly larger than the arm's base radius and orienting it along the arm's tangent so it blends naturally with the bone structure.

Still refining cuff geometry...

Now I'm figuring out cuff placement along each arm—4 cuffs per arm spaced between t=0.12 and 0.7, giving 80 small parts total across all arms. Next I need to work out the sucker placement.

Actually clock 180 is the belly, which stays hidden on dipping tubes but visible on raised arms and curled tips, so I should shift the suckers to around ±50° off the belly to catch visibility from the sides. I'm also worried cream cups on the cream underside sector would be too low-contrast, so I'll give the cups an orange or pale pink tint to stand out.

Now I'm settling on a palette: navy, blue, and light blue for the main body, a soft cyan for the belly, cream for the cups, orange for the accent sucker centers, and gunmetal tones for trim, plus a teal water color and white foam.

I'm deciding to keep the cups cream rather than orange so the accent color stays distinct. For the tentacle tips, I'm planning to add an orange glowing band or glow sphere at the tip to cap the spike with a luminous accent.

Now I'm thinking through mantle details—ribs, glow strips, a dorsal crest, fins, collar, and nodes—plus considering adding angled pauldron-like plates where the mantle meets the head, and gill-slit vents with orange glow along the flanks as a decal detail.

I'm also tallying overall part counts: using paint for belly sections instead of separate sectors keeps each tentacle to a single mesh, and I'm estimating texture density needed given the roughly 100 m² of painted surface across the body and arms.

For the water, I'm deciding against a flat untextured color since large plain surfaces read as unfinished -- instead I'll paint concentric ripple rings with noise by radius, though that roughly doubles the painted area to about 98 m². I'll stick with a 2048 paint size, accepting a coarser texel density of around 8mm per texel as an acceptable tradeoff.

Setting up imports and components...

Still defining color zones and seam darkening logic...

Still defining the mantle radius keys...

I'm setting up the spine chain from the mantle points as a catmull-rom curve attached to the core, with six joints running from base to tip, then starting on the head geometry as a sphere primitive.

Positioning the head ellipsoid so it protrudes forward of the mantle, matching paint gradients by normal angle so the seam between mantle and head blends well, then beginning a collar ring to bridge the gap between head and mantle.

Now I'm placing gunmetal loop rings around the mantle at each spinal joint to create rib-like segmentation, cutting cleanly across the mantle surface while leaving the head blob untouched since the sweep only covers the mantle. I'm working out which joint indices along the six-span chain correspond to evenly spaced positions for these rib loops.

I realize the collar ring at joint index 1 would partially overlap the head sphere, hiding part of it, so I'm shifting the collar to joint index 2 just above the head top, then placing ribs at indices 3, 4, and 5 where the mantle tapers from thick to thin.

I'm figuring out how to sample position and orientation along the chain for each loop using a frame (point plus tangent), so ribs land at parameter values 0.42, 0.55, 0.68, 0.8, with thin orange glow loops offset slightly further along at each point, and I still need to verify the collar's exact position at t=0.33 against the head's height through preview.

Now I'm working out the glow strips along the flanks: placing symmetric lines at angles roughly ±28-40 degrees with a small lift and radius so the glow sits right over the painted accent region, while making the paint itself a darker navy groove underneath so the two don't just duplicate each other.

For the dorsal crest, I'm thinking through how to build a membrane fin between two swept edges rather than a flat constant-height shape—considering tapering plates or a scalloped sail silhouette so it reads as a proper crest instead of a stiff fin.

For the crest coloring, I'm thinking a gradient from navy near the base transitioning to light blue, with an orange tip near the edge to give that Overwatch-ish accent look.

For height I'm defining a curve that rises smoothly over a parameter range, shaped like a tapered sine bump concentrated toward the back portion of the crest. Now I'm working out which side of the tilted tube faces world-up, since the mantle leans back and I need to figure out which perpendicular direction corresponds to the front-upper face versus the rear.

Thinking about cephalopod anatomy for clock-position mapping: the mantle's dorsal side faces up-back while the ventral belly faces forward toward the viewer, so I want dark navy stripes on the back-facing side and cream/cyan belly tones on the front, with blue flanks along the sides for a consistent look.

I'm trying to track which side of the tube stays "front" versus "back" as the path tilts from vertical and bends backward, since the normal frame needs to stay continuous through that transition rather than flipping discontinuously.

I should sidestep the ambiguity by basing the paint on world-space normals instead of the tangent frame—using normal-dot-dorsalDirection for the mantle angle, and world up/down for tentacles since they float near the surface, while keeping seams tied to the original s-coordinate for continuity.

Rather than reasoning this through further, it's probably faster to just test numerically: sample the surface at a few known angles, print the resulting normals, and see which direction actually corresponds to dorsal. I should check whether there's a quick way to run a throwaway script—maybe via the existing preview tooling or a scratch script runner—so let me peek at how the project's scripts are set up.

input.command: cat package.json | head -40; ls scripts samples scratch 2>/dev/null | head -30; which bun tsx node
